A mononuclear copper complex as bifunctional electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and water oxidation
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jelechem.2021.115106 Received 22 November 2020; Received in revised form 1 February 2021; Accepted 21 February 2021 Available online 09 March 2021 1572-6657/© 2021 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved.

Ning-ning Shi a,1, Wang-jing Xie a,1, Dong-mei Zhang a, Yu-Hua Fan a, Lian-Sheng Cui b,⇑, Mei Wang a,⇑ aKey Laboratory of Marine Chemistry Theory and Technology, Ministry of Education, College of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering, Ocean University of China, Qingdao, Shandong 266100, PR China bCollege of Chemistry and Environmental Engineering, Baise University, Baise, Guangxi 533000, PR China
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: Bifunctional electrocatalyst Copper complex Dpk ligand Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction Homogeneous calalysis Water oxidation
To mimic natural photosynthesis, it is still a great challenge to couple catalytic CO2 reduction and water oxidation in one single system with high activity. In this work, we have successfully synthesized and characterized a tetra-coordinated mononuclear copper complex [CuIIL2](ClO4)2·2CH3OH (1) (L = methoxy-di-pyridin-2-ylmethanol) with planar configuration, which can simultaneously serve as an efficient molecular electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and water oxidation. The copper complex displayed electrochemical activity for the reduction of CO2 to CO in DMF solution with the Faraday efficiency (FE) reached ~85% and a turnover frequency (TOF) of 2.99 s−1 in the presence of proton donor water. Meanwhile, it also can perform electrocatalytic water oxidation with the FE of ~86% and a high TOF of 9.20 s−1 at the pH of 11.84. The high electrochemical activity of complex 1 for the reduction of CO2 and water oxidation may due to the hydroxyl group on the methoxy-dipyridin-2-yl-methanol ligand. It represents the first copper complex as homogeneously bifunctional electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and water oxidation.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 to carbon-based fuels and water splitting for hydrogen production are considered as effective ways to solve the energy crisis and environmental issues [1–4]. Besides, to mimic natural photosynthesis in green plants which provides the energy and oxygen for our world, integrating catalytic CO2 reduction and water oxidation in one single system could enable us to produce renewable fuel efficiently [5–8]. On the other hand, as a half reaction, water oxidation can supply multiple electrons and protons for hydrogen evolution as well as carbon dioxide reduction. However, both the reactions of CO2 reduction and water oxidation have high kinetic barriers and high thermodynamic potentials. Thus, developing inexpensive, robust, and efficient bifunctional electrocatalyst for both CO2 reduction and water oxidation has become an increasingly important research pursuit.
In comparison to heterogeneous electrocatalyst, homogeneous catalysts have the advantages of illustrating the detailed mechanisms and easily tunable electronic and geometric parameters [9]. In the past few years, many non-precious transition metal complexes have been explored as excellent catalysts for water oxidation [10,11] and for
CO2 reduction [12–15], respectively. Nevertheless, only a few homogeneous catalysts have been reported for driving carbon dioxide reduction and water oxidation simultaneously and efficiently. In 2012, Meyer’s group reported a first RuII-based molecular electrocatalyst which could perform both CO2 reduction and water oxidation in CH3CN-H2O mixtures [16]. Wang et al demonstrated a series of stable molecular cubane catalysts Co4O4 with tunable redox potentials by the ligand modifications, while they found they could efficiently photocatalyze water oxidation and CO2 reduction simultaneously [17]. Colbran and co-workers developed two similar RuII molecular electrocatalysts for both CO2 reduction and water oxidation, meanwhile they found that the phenCO2− co-ligand plays crucial roles [18].
Di(2-pyridyl) ketone (dpk) is a promising ligand with three potential donor groups, two pyridine nitrogen atoms and one carbonyl oxygen atom, which could lead to mono- [19,20], bi- [21], and multinuclear complexes [22] and support various architectures. Hence, with strong π-accepting ability, the redox-active ligand dpk offers excellent potential in the application of catalysts. McKenzie reported the first rhenium-carbonyl compound containing dpk ligand which could react with CO2, resulting in a possible electrocatalytic pathway for CO2 reduction [23]. Chen [24] and Najafpour [25] demonstrated a
mononuclear cobalt complex with dpk ligand could perform photocatalytic and electrocatalytic water oxidation, respectively. Ding’s group [26] isolated an octanuclear Cu(II) cluster with dpk ligand, which has the highest TON and TOF values of 178 and 3.6 s−1 amongst all of the Cu-based photocatalytic water oxidation catalysts. Patzke’s group thoroughly investigated how to apply dpk ligand in Co(II)and Ni(II) systems by tuning with various counteranions to prepare different kinds of cubane molecular catalysts for water oxidation [27]. However, there has been no copper complexes acting as bifunctional electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and water oxidation.
For the reasons above, herein, we synthesized a mononuclear copper complex using di(2-pyridyl) ketone (dpk) as ligand, [CuL2](ClO4)2·2CH3OH (1) (L = Methoxy-di-pyridin-2-yl-methanol) and investigated its application in electrocatalysis. Through profound exploration, it is found that the copper complex could efficiently electrocatalyze CO2 reduction and water oxidation simultaneously. Its high stability during the two whole catalytic processes has also been proved by a series of investigations.

sections.heading: 2.1. General procedures
sections.text: Unless otherwise stated, all manipulations were carried out under argon or carbon dioxide atmosphere, and all chemicals were commercially available and used as supplied without further purification, carbon dioxide and argon were purchased from Deihai Gases Corporation.

sections.heading: 2.2. Synthesis
sections.text: A methanol (20 mL) solution of di(2-pyridyl) ketone (92 mg, 0.5 mmol) and Cu(ClO4)2·6H2O (131 mg, 0.5 mmol) was stirred for 2 h at room temperature under aerobic conditions, then 0.05 mmol of triethylamine was added. After stirring for another 3 h, the resulting purple solution was filtrated. X-ray quality purple crystals were obtained by diffusing diethyl ether into the filtrate. The purple crystals were washed with ether and dried in vacuo. C24H24CuN4O4(ClO4)2·2 (CH4O): calcd. C 41.14, H 4.22, N 3.38; found C 41.26, H 4.30, N 7.49.

sections.heading: 2.3. Physical measurements
sections.text: Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) data were measured with a RIGAKU DMAX2500PC diffractometer with Cu-Ka radiation (k = 1.54056 Å). DLS (dynamic light scattering) experiments were performed using a NanoBrook Omni Dynamic Light Scattering (DLS) particle sizer and zeta potential analyzer (particle size distribution from 0.3 to 104 nm). Single crystal of 1 was mounted on a Bruker SMART APEX II CCD X-ray single-crystal diffractometer, and all data were collected at 173 K with graphite monochromated MoKɑ radiation (λ = 0.71073 Å) in I > 2σ(I) diffraction spots and reduced by the SAINT program, and absorption corrections were applied using program SADABS [28]. CCDC for the complex is 1955151. The crystal pattern of the as-synthesized complex was detected by comparing its experimental and theoretical powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns (Fig. S1). The peak positions of the diffraction in patterns are all in good agreement, which confirms that the crystalline phases of all the as-prepared samples are all uniform.

sections.heading: 2.4. Electrochemical measurements and electrolysis product analysis
sections.text:
All electrochemical experiments were tested by a CHI660E electrochemical analyzer to study their electrocatalytic properties and performed in a single chamber three-electrode reactor. 0.1 M solution of nBu4NPF6 in DMF was used as supporting electrolyte. Cyclic voltammogram (CV) experiments and control potential electrolysis (CPE)
were performed with F-doped tin oxide (FTO) conducting glass substrates (1 cm 1 cm, active surface area was 1.0 cm2) as the working electrode, which was obtained from Zhuhai Kaivo Optoelectronic Corp. They were pre-treated by dipping them in 5 wt% NaOH in ethanol for several hours, and then cleaning with water, ethanol, and water successively. There was about 10 mL of solution in the electrolytic cell, and the concentration of the complexes in the solution was about 0.5 mmol/L. The counter-electrode was a platinum wire and the reference electrode was Ag/AgCl electrode. Before each experiment the solution was purged with Ar or CO2 for 30 min at room temperature. The pH values of the buffer were adjusted by adding 0.1 M NaOH or 0.1 M HAc in sodium acetate.
The in situ UV–Vis spectroelectrochemistry was carried out by using a UV-1800 UV–vis spectrophotometer (Shimadzu). In situ spectroelectrochemical studies were performed using a quartz cuvette of 1 cm path length assembled as an electrochemical cell, containing a platinum gauze, a platinum wire and an Ag/AgCl (saturated KCl) electrode as working, counter and reference electrode, respectively. For the CO2 reduction, the headspace gas samples (1 mL) generated by CPE experiments were extracted using a lure lock-type air-tight syringe and injected into a gas chromatography instrument (GC, Shimadzu GC2014) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) with mechanizer to analyze CO and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD, Shimadzu) to perform analysis for quantifying H2. Ultra-high purity Ar was used as carrier gas to detect CO and H2. For the water oxidation reaction, an Ocean Optics NeoFox-GT oxygen probe was adopted to quantify the generated oxygen concentration in the solution and in the headspace. However, after electrolysis, the concentration of the headspace oxygen was below the detection limit of the sensor.

sections.heading: 2.5. Density functional theory calculations
sections.text: Quantum-mechanical calculations were carried out using the Gaussian 09 program package, using the B3LYP hybrid functional [29] and the “double-ξ” quality LanL2DZ [30] basis sets were used for transition metals Cu and 6-311G (d, p) basis sets were used for non-metal atoms [31]. Atom coordinates used in the calculations were from crystallographic data, and the solvent was modelled.

sections.heading: 3.1. Synthesis
sections.text: In the synthesis of coordination compounds for various research fields, the ligand di(2-pyridyl) ketone (dpk) and its derivatives have been widely employed [32]. In the process of synthesis, as shown in scheme 1, the ketocarbonyl group of the dpk ligand could undergo metal-promoted solvation, resulting in four possible donor sites (N, N0, O, O0) on the ligand which can support numbers of sorts of complexes with different coordination modes [33]. Besides, dpk ligand in the synthesized complex could serve as a redox-active ligand to assist catalytic reactions [34]. Hence, we attempted to synthesize copper complexes using dpk as the ligand for elcectrocatalytic CO2 reduction and water oxidation catalyst. A series of experiments have been explored by trying different kinds of copper salt, solvent, reaction temperature etc. Eventually, by using Cu(ClO4)2·6H2O as the salt resource, methanol as the solvent, we successfully isolated a tetra-coordinated CuII complex with two methanol solvated dpk ligands dpk·MeOH.

sections.heading: 3.2. Characterization of the crystal structures
sections.text:
Single-crystal X-ray diffraction analysis shows that complex 1 crystallizes in the monoclinic system with centrosymmetric space group P21/c (Table S1). The structure of the monocation in crystals of
complex 1 is shown in Fig. 1, while the selected bond angles are listed in Table S2.
Based on the bond valence sum calculations, the copper atom in the complex is in +2 oxidation state [35]. As depicted in Fig. 1, the central CuII ion is four-coordinated by four pyridyl N atoms, which are from two methanol solvated dpk derivatives dpk·CH3OH. The bond lengths of Cu1-N1 and Cu1-N2 are 2.007(4) and 2.000(4) Å, respectively, which are comparable with that reported for Cu(II) tetra-coordinated complexes [36,37]. The largest angles (N1A-Cu1-N1, N2ACu1-N2) in the complexes are all 180°. The four N atoms all lie in one planar to form an almost square configuration with the geometry index τ4 equals zero, where τ4 = 360°-(α + β)/141°, α and β are the two largest angles in the compounds [38,39].

sections.heading: 3.3. Electrochemical properties of complex 1
sections.text: Fig. 2 shows the cyclic voltammetry (CV) of complex 1, recorded in DMF solution under 1 atm Ar atmosphere (all potential versus NHE). As scanning towards the cathode potential, it presents three irreversible reduction peaks at −0.17 V, −0.79 V, −1.24 V. The first reduction wave could be assigned to CuII/CuI couple. While the second and the third reduction waves could be attributed to the two identical ligands dpk reduction dpk/dpk·−, which is a little more positive than that of the dpk/dpk·− couple for the free ligand (−0.92 V) [23,40]. This is consistent with the reported data for copper complexes that the coordinated ligands are reduced at more positive potentials than those of the free ligands [41]. Meanwhile, five oxidation peaks were observed at the potentials of −1.22 V, − 0.77 V, −0.22 V, 1.16 V, 1.44 V in the anodic sweep, of which the first two oxidation waves should be assigned to the two ligand coulple dpk·−/dpk and the last three oxidation waves can be attributed to CuI/CuII, CuII/CuIII, CuIII/ CuIV couples, respectively. In addition, as shown in the inset of Fig. 2, the peak currents ip corresponding to the three reduction and two oxidation potentials in DMF solution, all have good linear relationships with the square root of scan rates v1/2, indicating that these five processes are diffusion-controlled.

sections.heading: 3.4. Study on electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide by complex 1
sections.text:
In order to investigate the electrocatalytic reduction activity for carbon dioxide by complex 1, the electrochemical properties were
tested under saturated CO2 with 0.1 M nBu4NPF6 as supporting electrolyte in DMF solution by performing cyclic voltammetry experiments and controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) on F-doped tin oxide conducting glass (FTO) electrode. As illustrated in Fig. 3, it was found that compared with those under Ar atmosphere at the same scan rate, the CV plots for complex 1 under saturated CO2 show largely enhanced reductive waves around −0.28 V and −1.04 V in DMF solution. In addition, by employing control potential electrolysis (CPE), CO can be detected by GC analysis at the two potentials in DMF solution, which indicates that complex 1 can electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to CO in DMF solution at the two potentials. The cyclic voltammetry experiment for complex 1 under saturated carbon dioxide atmosphere in DMF solution was also recorded at different scan rates shown in Fig. 4. It can be found that all the CV plots at different scan rates repeated well with no evolution of new oxidative or the reductive waves, which assure the reproducibility and stability of the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction for complex 1. Meanwhile, the relationship between concentrations of the complex and the catalytic current peaks were also investigated (Fig. 5), which reveals that the catalytic currents at the cathode potentials of −0.28 V and −1.04 V both have linear dependence relationship with catalyst concentrations, proving that the rate determining step in the catalysis is the first order.
Based on the half peak potential of the CVs (Eapplied = -0.28 V, −1.04 V in the Equation (1)), the overpotentials (η) where the electrocatalytic CO2 reduction happens for the complex 1 are around 238 and 998 mV, respectively, in which E0CO2=COðDMFÞ equals −0.042 V vs NHE [42].

F is Faraday’s constant (96485C mol−1), v is the scan rate employed (0.1 V s−1), np is the number of electrons involved in the non-catalytic redox reaction (np = 1), R is the gas constant (8.314 J K−1 mol−1), T is the temperature (293.15 K) and ncat is the number of electrons involved for the catalytic reaction (ncat = 2 for the reduction of CO2 to CO, or the evolution of H2), ip and icat are determined as the peak current under Ar and CO2 respectively. The calculated TOF without adding proton sources is 1.39 s−1 (icat/ip = 2.65) in DMF solution at the potential of −0.28 V and 1.48 s−1 (icat/ip = 2.73) at the potential of −1.04 V which is higher than [44–47] or comparable [48,49] to those of many reported
molecular CO2 reduction catalysts. The high catalytic reactivity for CO2 reduction of complex 1 may be owning to the two hydroxyl groups on the two methoxy-di-pyridin-2-yl-methanol ligands which could help the formation and stabilization of the intermediates [50–52].
In order to investigate the activity of electrocatalytic reduction of carbon dioxide in the presence of proton donor system, distilled water
and TFE (trifluoroethanol) were continuously added to the catalytic system under the same conditions (0.1 M of nBu4NPF6 in DMF solution), respectively. The magnitude of the catalytic currents at the potential of −1.04 V both increase (Fig. 6 and Fig. S2), as adding the proton source H2O and TFE to the electrolyte solution, respectively. Moreover, the catalytic peak potentials shift to anode slightly when the concentration of the proton source H2O and TFE raise from 0.56 to 3.33 M and 0.20 to 3.50 M, respectively.
According to the GC analysis, the calculated Faraday efficiency (FE) of CO evolution for complex in DMF solution are shown in Fig. 7. The Faraday efficiency of CO for complex 1 in DMF solution without proton source could reach approximately 14%, 63% during the whole electrolysis of 2000 s at the applied potentials of −0.28 V, −1.04 V, respectively. Upon the addition of a proton source, the FE of CO formation increased significantly while the Faraday efficiency of H2 decreased at both the applied potentials of −0.28 V, −1.04 V. The FE of CO evolution reaches about 47%, 85% under the same conditions except with the addition of 1.11 M H2O as a proton source, which is higher than the reported mononuclear copper complex [53,54] implying that the addition of proton source can accelerate the catalysis and the Faraday efficiency. In addition, the calculated TOF with adding proton source is 1.56 s−1 (icat/ip = 2.81) in DMF solution at the potential of −0.28 V and 2.99 s−1 (icat/ip = 3.89) at the potential of −1.04 V, which is higher than the same condition except with the addition of 1.1 M H2O, further indicated that the addition of proton source can accelerate the catalysis and the TOF. In order to study the stability of the catalyst, a series of experiments have been performed. The current densities for complex 1 at the potentials of −0.28 V and −1.04 V both stabilized during 2000 s electrolysis period, indicating that the catalyst remained stable in solution throughout the catalytic process (Fig. 8). Besides, DLS (dynamic light scatting) of complex 1 before and after 2000 s electrolysis in DMF solution (Figs. S3a and S3b) were performed, which reveals that the particle distribution is in the range of the molecular hydrodynamic diameter of the cluster, indicating that there are no nanoparticles formed during electrolysis. In addition, as presented in Fig. S4, the in situ UV–vis spectroelectrochemistry for complex 1 in DMF solution was performed during controlled potential electrolysis, while there are few differences in the spectrum, which further confirm the high stability of complex 1 during electrolysis. Furthermore, it was found that there was no electrodeposited film on the glass electrode by comparing the scanning electron microscope (SEM) images (Fig. S5) of the fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) transparent conductive glass electrode of the complex, which further confirmed that the complex has certain catalysis stability. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed that there have been no metal-oxide formed after the CO2 reduction electrolysis (Fig. S6), which revealed that complex 1 is quite stable during the 2000 s electrolysis.

sections.heading: 3.5. Study on electrocatalytic performance of water oxidation of complex 1
sections.text:
In order to investigate the catalytic oxidation properties of complex 1, CVs were measured in sodium acetate buffer solution prepared by distilled water at different pH values under 1 atm Ar. It is found that the irreversible oxidative peak waves at around 1.5 V display largely enhanced (Fig. 9) and the current peak values at the potential of ~1.50 V increase with the pH raising from 7.81 to 11.84, all of which reveal that complex 1 can catalyze water oxidation at Ep = ~1.50 V in sodium acetate aqueous solution. Meanwhile, the linear relationship between the complex concentrations and the catalytic current peaks (Fig. 10) indicates that the rate determining step in the water oxidation catalysis is the first order. Furthermore, the onset potentials for water oxidation display pH-dependence (the inset of Fig. 11) with a slope of 53 mV pH−1, which indicates that it could be a PCET (proton-coupled electron transfer) electrocatalytic process.
Based on the half peak potential of the CVs (Ereal(O2/H2O) in the Equation (4)), the overpotentials (ƞ) where the electrocatalytic water oxidation happens for complex 1 are 602–909 mV in the pH range of 7.81–11.84, respectively, which is defined by Eqs. (3) and (4).

The calculated TOF of electrocatalytic water oxidation is 0.28 s−1 at pH = 7.81 and 9.20 s−1 at pH = 11.84 using the slope of the plot of icat/ip versus v−1/2 (the inset of Fig. 12, the raw data in the inner illustration of Fig. 12 are all from Table S3), which is much higher than the reported copper molecular water oxidation catalysts [4,56–58]. The high TOF value may because the hydroxyl group on the two methanol solvated dpk ligand dpk·MeOH participate in the four electron transfer process and assist proton-coupled electron transfer [4,59,60].
To explore the electrocatalytic activity of complex 1 for water oxidation, controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) experiments were tested at the potential of 1.5 V and 1.75 V at pH = 7.81 and pH = 11.84 in a gas-tight cell under the same condition. As shown in Fig. 13, under the condition of pH = 7.81, at the applied potential of 1.75 and 1.5 V, the detected dissolved O2 concentration reaches to 109 and 78 μM, and the current density is about 0.5 and 0.4 mA cm−2, leading to the Faraday efficiency of ~84% and 75%, respectively. In addition, at pH = 11.84, at the applied potential of 1.75 and 1.5 V, the detected dissolved O2 concentration reaches to 151 and 121 μM, meanwhile the current density is about 0.61 and 0.58 mA cm−2, resulting in the faraday efficiency of ~86% and 80%, respectively, of which the Faraday efficiencies are higher than those of near neutral condition. Meanwhile, the oxygen content is close to zero and the current density is very small at 0.06 mA cm−2 without complex 1, indicating that there is no catalysis occurred in the absence of complex 1. Meanwhile the current densities are −0.58, −0.61, −0.77 mA cm−2 for complex 1 at −1.70 V, −1.75 V, −1.80 V under the condition of pH = 11.84 (Fig. S8). The detected dissolved O2 concentration are 128, 151 and 45 μM, leading to the Faraday efficiency of 85%, 86% and 23%, respectively. Moreover, rinse test was performed on the FTO electrode after the whole electrocatalysis, the dissolved O2 and the current density are very closed to the blank test, which indicates that complex 1 is homogeneous catalyst. Besides, DLS (dynamic light scatting) analyses of the complex were investigated before and after 2000 s electrolysis in 0.1 M acetate buffer which reveal that the particle distribution is in the range of the molecular hydrodynamic diameter of the cluster (Fig. S9a and S9b), indicating that there are no nanoparticles formed

In addition, as presented in Fig. S10, the in situ UV–vis spectroelectrochemistry for the complex in 0.1 M acetate buffer solution was performed for 2000 s during controlled potential electrolysis, while there are quite a few differences in the spectrum, which further prove the high stability of the complex during electrolysis. Furthermore, it is found that there is no electrodeposited film on the glass electrode by comparing the scanning electron microscope (SEM)
images (Fig. S11) of the fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) transparent conductive glass electrode of the complex, which further confirm that the complex has high catalytic stability. In addition, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed that there have been no metaloxide formed after the water oxidation electrolysis (Fig. S12), which revealed that complex 1 is quite stable during the 2000 s electrolysis.
To elucidate the charge transfer resistance of the two process of complex 1. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS)
measurements were conducted of 1 and CuII(bipy)2SO4 by using a CHI660E electrochemical analyzer. The impedance spectra were recorded between 100 kHz and 10 mHz with the amplitude of the ac signal at 5 mV.
On the basis of the equivalent circuit shown in the inset of Fig. S13, we fitted the impedance spectra with Z-view software and the corresponding parameters extracted from the Nyquist plots are listed in Table S4.
The variable R1 represents the electrolyte resistance, CPE1 is the double-layer capacitance at the electrode interface where the roughness of the electrode surface may result in a deviation from a pure capacitor, R2 is the charge transfer resistance, and W1 denotes the Warburg-type diffusion of the redox-active species to the electrode surface [61–63].
As the fitted parameters presented in Table S4, complex 1 exhibits lower values of solution resistance (R1 = 3.50 Ω, 6.83 Ω) and lower charge transfer resistance (R2 = 43.47 Ω, 119.2 Ω) than those of CuII(bipy)2SO4 (R1 = 16.97 Ω, 14.49 Ω; R2 = 224.5 Ω, 204.9 Ω) in CO2 reduction process and water oxidation process, respectively, which illustrates that complex 1 possesses the faster electron-transport ability to enhance electrocatalytic CO2 reduction and water oxidation.
To explore the role of –OH group in mononuclear copper complex, CuII(bipy)2SO4 was synthesized according to the adaptation of the reported literatures [64,65]. All electrochemical experiments were tested by a CHI660E electrochemical analyzer to study their electrocatalytic properties and performed in a single chamber three-electrode reactor. Cyclic voltammogram (CV) experiments and control potential electrolysis (CPE) were performed with F-doped tin oxide (FTO) conducting glass substrates (1 cm 1 cm, active surface area was
1.0 cm2) as the working electrode, which was obtained from Zhuhai Kaivo Optoelectronic Corp. They were pre-treated by dipping them in 5 wt% NaOH in ethanol for several hours, and then cleaning with water, ethanol, and water successively. There was about 10 mL of solution in the electrolytic cell, and the concentration of the complexes in the solution was about 0.5 mmol/L. The counter-electrode was a platinum wire and the reference electrode was Ag/AgCl electrode. Before each experiment the solution was purged with Ar or CO2 for 30 min at room temperature. The pH values of the buffer were adjusted by adding 0.1 M NaOH or 0.1 M HAc in sodium acetate.
As shown in Fig. S14, the calculated TOF with the addition of 1.0 M TFE as proton source is 0.88 s−1 (icat/ip = 2.11) in 0.1 M KCl aqueous solution at the potential of −1.42 V. Meanwhile, the catalytic current is −1.11 mA cm−2 and the Faraday efficiency is ~9.2% (Fig. S15), which is lower than complex 1. In order to investigate the catalytic oxidation properties of CuII(bipy)2SO4, CVs were measured in sodium acetate buffer solution prepared by distilled water at different pH values under 1 atm Ar (Fig. S16). It is found that the current peak values at the potential of ~1.30 to 1.82 V increase with the pH raising from 7.46 to 13.01, then controlled potential electrolysis (CPE) experiments showed that the detected dissolved O2 concentration is 7 μM and the current density is 0.35 mA cm−2 (Fig. S17) with a low Faraday efficiency of 7.72% at 1.82 V and pH= 13.01. All of these results showed that the catalytic activity of CuII(bipy)2SO4 is much lower than that of complex 1, indicating that the high electrochemical activity of complex 1 for the reduction of CO2 and water oxidation may due to the hydroxyl group on the methoxy-di-pyridin-2-yl-methanol ligand.

sections.heading: 3.6. Density functional theory (DFT) calculations and proposed mechanism
sections.text:
DFT calculations have been conducted to evaluate the proposed mechanisms of electrocatalytic CO2 reduction and water oxidation by complex 1 (Schemes S1 and S2, respectively), while the optimized structures of the related species in the reaction pathways for complex 1 are summarized in Tables S5–S11.
A proposed mechanism for the reduction of CO2 to CO by 1 is illustrated in Scheme S1. Complex 1 is reduced by one electron to generate [CuIL2]+ (1a). Enhanced currents are observed at potentials near that for the Cu II/I couple upon addition of CO2, suggesting that [CuII(L2)] can bind the substrate to form [CuII(L2)(CO22−)]0 (1b). In the presence of protons this intermediate is converted into a metal-COOH species, [CuIIL2-COOH]+ (1c). Proton-promoted C–OH bond cleavage gives a carbonyl intermediate, which subsequently dissociates CO to regenerate the starting material 1.
The catalytic cycle for water oxidation is proposed in Scheme S2. The four coordinated compound 1 has two coordination vacancies, so that two molecules of water can bind to the Cu(II) metal center. Then the species [CuIIL2-OOH]− (2a) could be formed [4]. The resulting [CuIIL2-OOH]− was oxidized to the intermediate [CuIIIL2-OO]− (2b) via a PCET process (1H+/1e−). Subsequently, the high-valence copper intermediate [CuIIIL2-OO]− was attacked by H2O, resulting in the formation of the intermediate [CuIVL2-OO-OH]− (2c), which should be the rate-limiting OAO bond formation step process. Eventually, the intermediate [CuIVL2-OOOH]− releases the oxygen molecule, and generated the initial species [CuIIL2-OOH]− for next catalytic cycle.
In the process of CO2 reduction, [CuIIL2]2+(1) is reduced by one electron to generate [CuIL2]+ (1a), then [CuII(L2)] can bind the substrate to form a serial of intermediates, leading to the release of CO. Meanwhile, in the process of water oxidation, two molecules of water bind to the Cu(II) metal center to form several intermediates during the oxidation of the cooper ions, resulting in the evolution of the oxygen. All of which indicated that the Cu metal center in mononuclear copper complex could combine with the catalytic substrate (CO2 or H2O) to form different intermediates, as well as transfer electrons
and protons, and finally complete the catalytic CO2 reduction or water oxidation process with the cooperation of the ligands.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In this study, we have demonstrated a mononuclear copper complex [CuIIL2](ClO4)2·2CH3OH (L =Methoxy-di-pyridin-2-yl-methanol) with tetra-coordinated planar conformation, which can act as homogeneously bifunctional electrocatalyst for CO2 reduction and water oxidation. Bulk electrichemical investigation reveals that the copper complex can electrocatalyze CO2 reduction to CO with the FE of ~85% and a TOF of 2.99 s−1 with addition of 1.11 M H2O as a proton source in DMF solution, in the meantime, it also has great performance for electrocatalytic water oxidation with a FE of ~86% and a high TOF of 9.20 s−1 at the pH of 11.84. The high catalytic reactivity for CO2 reduction and water oxidation of complex 1 could be attributed to the two hydroxyl groups on the two methoxy-di-pyridin-2-yl-methanol ligands for assisting the formation and stabilization of the intermediates and proton-coupled electron transfer, respectively. A series of electrochemical investigations combining with DLS analysis, in-situ UV–Vis spectroelectrochemistry, rinsing test and SEM assure that complex 1 can homogeneously catalyze both CO2 reduction and water oxidation with high stability. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first example of copper complex as bifunctional electrocatalyst for both CO2 reduction and water oxidation. This work serves valuable perception for exploring non-noble transition metal complexes as bifunctional electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction and water oxidation.
